newsitem.title: USA: House panel backs "Kidcare" and health savings.
newsitem.headline: House panel backs "Kidcare" and health savings.

text.p: A House subcommittee late Tuesday endorsed creating a new $16 billion "KidCare" initiative to cover uninsured poor children and backed billions of dollars of savings in Medicare and Medicaid.
The House Commerce health subcommittee in a bipartisan voice vote backed "KidCare", which could cover up to half the nation's 10 million uninsured children over five years.

The bill provides $2.6 billion a year in grants to states for "KidCare." The programme would be voluntary and states would have to kick in money of their own. But they would have latitude in designing their programmes, which could include vouchers, managed care, direct aid or other methods.
In addition, states could expand Medicaid to reach more children, including those in families with incomes up to 150 percent of poverty, about $25,000 for a family of four.

Despite the cooperation on children's health, partisan disputes about Medicare and Medicaid were plentiful in nearly 14 hours of debate that ended just seconds before midnight. Most Democrats opposed both plans as written by the Republican-controlled committee.
The spending goals -- cutting $115 billion from Medicare and $15 billion from Medicaid -- are central items in the balanced budget accord between Congress and the White House.
But Democrats said the Republicans failed to live up to some of the promises in the budget accord, particularly by falling short on a pledge to subsidise Medicare premiums for the poor elderly.
Medicare covers everyone over 65, but people do have to pay a fee for the portion of the programme that covers doctors visits and similar health expenses.
"This is a false promise," Frank Pallone, a New Jersey Democrat, said. "I think clearly the deal is broken here."
But subcommittee chairman Michael Bilirakis, a Florida Republican, said the only way the panel could come up with more money for premiums was by taking it away from hospitals that care for the poor.

Medicare savings come primarily from restraining payments to hospitals, managed care plans and other health providers. The revamped programme also gives seniors more choices of health maintenance organisations and other forms of managed care.

In addition, it introduces a pilot programme of tax-free Medical Savings Accounts, which Republicans say will promote wise health spending and Democrats say will undermine Medicare. Democrats tried repeatedly to strike it, and wanted to use the money for the Medicare premium subsidies.

Most of the savings from Medicaid, a joint federal-state health insurance programme for the poor, come from reducing the "disproportionate share" or "DSH" payments to hospitals that treat many poor and uninsured people.

The budget agreement called for $15 billion in Medicaid savings but a few Republicans joined the Democrats to block the repeal of a measure, known as the Boren amendment, that guarantees certain levels of payments to nursing homes.
Restoring the Boren amendment cut savings by about $1 billion, a shortfall the full Commerce committee will address when it considers Medicare and Medicaid later this week.
The panel, generally with bipartisan support, backed several amendments that would curtail what critics of managed care have called abuses or possible room for abuse.

They voted to ensure that doctors, not managed care company employees, would determine how long a patient stayed in the hospital and barred "gag rules" that would prevent a doctor from disclosing all treatment options.
